title: Newton's Laws of Motion & Friction
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Inertial & Non-Inertial Frames, Free Body Diagrams (FBD), Constraint Equations, Pseudo Force, Friction & Circular Turning Dynamics
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Causes Motion?

In Chapters 02 and 03 (Kinematics), we described how things move. In Chapter 04 (Dynamics), we answer the fundamental question: Why do things move or accelerate?

Newton's Breakthrough:
Aristotle believed that a constant force was required to keep an object moving at a constant speed. Sir Isaac Newton shattered this misconception with his First Law: An object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by a net external force to change that state!

topics.title: Newton's Three Laws of Motion, Linear Momentum & Free Body Diagram (FBD) Master Rules
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Newton's Three Laws & Conservation of Linear Momentum
LawStatementMaster Formula
First LawLaw of Inertia: Natural tendency to resist change in state of motion.$\sum \vec{F} = 0 \iff \vec{v} = \text{constant}$
Second LawRate of change of linear momentum is directly proportional to net external force.$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = m\vec{a}$ (if $m$ is constant)
Third LawTo every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction (acting on two different bodies!).$\vec{A\text{on}B} = -\vec{B\text{on}A}$
$$\textbf{Conservation of Linear Momentum:} \quad \text{If } \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0 \implies \boxed{\vec{p} = \text{constant} \implies m_1 \vec{u}_1 + m_2 \vec{u}_2 = m_1 \vec{v}_1 + m_2 \vec{v}_2}$$
1.2 The 4-Step Golden Rule for Drawing Free Body Diagrams (FBD)
  1. Step 1: Isolate the single body of interest and represent it as a point dot.
  2. Step 2: Identify and draw all real physical contact and field forces acting ON that body (Gravity $mg$ downward, Normal force $N$ perpendicular outward from contact surfaces, Tension $T$ pulling away along strings, Friction).
  3. Step 3: Choose a smart coordinate axis (e.g., parallel and perpendicular to an inclined plane or string path).
  4. Step 4: Apply $\sum F_x = m a_x$ and $\sum F_y = m a_y$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Recoil Speed of a Gun When Firing Bullets:

By Conservation of Linear Momentum in an isolated system ($\vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$):

$$0 = m_b v_b + M_g v_g \implies \boxed{v_g = -\frac{m_b v_b}{M_g}}$$

topics.title: String & Wedge Constraints, Pulley Systems & Pseudo Force in Non-Inertial Frames
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 String Constraint Equation (Work Method)
$$\textbf{For any inextensible string of fixed length:} \quad \sum (T \cdot x) = \text{constant} \implies \sum (T \cdot a) = 0$$
2.2 Pseudo Force in Non-Inertial (Accelerating) Frames
Definition:
When solving equations from the point of view of an observer accelerating at acceleration $\vec{a}_0$, you must apply a fictitious Pseudo Force $\vec{F}_{\text{pseudo}} = -m\vec{a}_0$ on every mass $m$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Atwood Machine Acceleration Derivation:

$$a = \left(\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)g, \qquad T = \frac{2m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$$

topics.title: Friction: Static, Kinetic, Angle of Repose, Cone of Friction & Minimum Pulling/Pushing Force
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Laws of Friction & Angle of Repose
Type of FrictionMaximum / Kinetic FormulaKey Characteristics
Static Friction ($f_s$)$f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$Self-adjusting force ($0 \le f_s \le \mu_s N$) that prevents slipping.
Kinetic Friction ($f_k$)$f_k = \mu_k N$Constant friction opposing relative sliding ($(\mu_k < \mu_s)$).
$$\textbf{Angle of Repose } (\lambda): \quad \boxed{\tan\lambda = \mu_s}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Minimum Force $F$ to Move a Block on Rough Floor at Angle θ:

$$F = \frac{\mu_s mg}{\cos\theta + \mu_s\sin\theta} \implies F_{\min} = \frac{\mu_s mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}} = mg\sin\lambda$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Static Friction Calculation): Never write $f_s = \mu_s N$ blindly! Static friction is self-adjusting; you must first calculate the required force from $\sum F = 0$ and check if it is less than $\mu_s N$.

topics.title: Circular Dynamics: Centripetal Force, Unbanked vs. Banked Curves & Vertical Loop Mechanics
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Minimum Speed at Top of Vertical Loop & String Slack Condition
$$\textbf{Critical Speed at Top of Vertical Loop (Tension } T \ge 0\text{):} \quad \boxed{v_{\min} = \sqrt{rg}}$$
$$\textbf{Minimum Speed at Bottom to Complete Loop:} \quad v_{\text{bottom}} = \sqrt{5rg}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Critical Top Speed in Vertical Loop:

$$T + mg = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$

Setting $T = 0$ (slack condition) gives $mg = \frac{mv_{\min}^2}{r} \implies v_{\min} = \sqrt{rg}$.

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Rod vs. String in Vertical Loop): If the bob is tied to a rigid massless rod instead of a string, it can pass the top with $v = 0$ without collapsing!

questions.prompt: A block of mass $m = 4\text{ kg}$ rests on a rough horizontal floor with static friction coefficient $\mu_s = 0.5$ and kinetic friction coefficient $\mu_k = 0.4$. A horizontal pulling force $F = 15\text{ N}$ is applied. What is the friction force acting on the block? ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.explanation: Maximum static friction is $f_{s,\max} = \mu_s mg = (0.5)(4)(10) = 20\text{ N}$. Since the applied pull $F = 15\text{ N}$ is less than $20\text{ N}$, the block does not move. By self-adjustment, static friction equals the applied pull: $f_s = 15\text{ N}$.

questions.prompt: A particle of mass $m$ is moving in a vertical circle of radius $r$ with critical speed at the highest point. What is the tension in the string when the particle is at the lowest point of the circle?
questions.explanation: By work-energy theorem between top and bottom, $v_{\text{bottom}}^2 = v_{\text{top}}^2 + 2g(2r) = rg + 4rg = 5rg$. At the bottom, $T - mg = \frac{mv_{\text{bottom}}^2}{r} = m(5g) \implies T = 6mg$.
